Harvest Robot Field Trial - Final Report
Prepared by Ines Carvalho, Fenwick Agritech, Oct 2026

Scope: The Pomona-4 apple-picking robot was trialed for 14 consecutive days across three orchards in the Yakima valley: Lindqvist Farms, Red Ridge, and Dunmore Orchard.

Results: The robot attempted 47,300 picks and successfully harvested 41,150 apples, a 87% success rate. A comparison crew of human pickers achieved 94% on the same rows. Bruising was detected on 3.1% of robot-picked fruit versus 2.4% for humans.

Economics: Estimated cost per kilogram harvested was $0.31 for the robot versus $0.27 for hand picking, assuming a 5-year depreciation. The gap narrows to $0.25 if night shifts are used, since the robot works in the dark with no lighting cost beyond the onboard lamps.

Reliability: There were 9 unplanned stops, 6 caused by battery swaps taking longer than planned and 3 by branch occlusion confusing the vision model. Mean time to recover was 11 minutes.

Farmer feedback: Lindqvist Farms rated the system 4 out of 5 and asked for a faster battery swap. Dunmore Orchard rated it 3 out of 5, citing trouble with dense canopies.

Recommendation: Expand to a 6-robot deployment in spring 2027 only if the vision model update cuts occlusion errors by half and the hot-swap battery is delivered by January.

emails.subject: Incident report: Cell 6 robot collision
emails.body:
Summary of the Oct 14 incident at Brandt Fabrication, Cell 6.

At 02:40 on Oct 14, the KR-210 welding robot in Cell 6 swung outside its programmed path and struck a clamping fixture. The emergency stop was triggered by the safety scanner within 0.4 seconds. No one was in the cell and there were no injuries.

Damage: The fixture was destroyed and the robot's wrist joint needed replacement. Parts and labor came to $23,400. The cell was down for 3 days, with an estimated lost output of 1,150 parts, which were made up on overtime.

Root cause: The investigation found that a firmware update on Oct 11 overwrote the tool calibration file with a stale copy from August. The robot therefore believed its welding torch was 38 mm shorter than it actually is, causing the path error. The operator checklist did not include a calibration verification step after updates.

Corrective actions: (1) Recalibrate all 9 robot arms on the floor by Nov 13. (2) Add a mandatory post-update calibration check to the checklist, effective Oct 26. (3) Back up calibration files nightly to the shared server. (4) Retrain night-shift operators on the e-stop review procedure on Nov 5.

Owner: Gwen Aldrich, Safety Manager. Please reach out with questions.

files./home/user/research/gripper_study.txt:
Soft Gripper Field Study - Ostrava Robotics Lab, Oct 2026
Lead: Dr. Pavel Novak.

Background: Warehouse pickers struggle with deformable items such as bagged goods. The lab tested a new three-finger soft gripper with pressure-adaptive pads against the standard rigid two-finger gripper.

Method: Each gripper attempted 1,200 picks over 10 days across 30 item types, including bags, boxes and bottles. Items were placed randomly in bins.

Results: The standard gripper succeeded in 76% of picks. The soft gripper succeeded in 91%. Drops during transport fell by 42%. Cycle time was slightly slower, 4.1 seconds per pick versus 3.6 seconds. Bottles were the hardest item for the soft gripper, with an 84% success rate.

Cost: The soft gripper costs about $1,350 per unit versus $900 for the rigid one. Pads need replacing after roughly 50,000 picks.

Conclusion: The soft gripper is recommended for mixed-item bins where success rate matters more than raw speed. A follow-up study on pad durability is planned for Q1 2027.
